entries.text: The Go Blog Go Turns 17 Austin Clements, for the Go team 10 November 2026 Today, November 10th, we celebrate the 17th anniversary of Go’s open source release! Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27 in August, alongside a steady stream of releases across our golang.org/x libraries and developer tools. Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems. In a tumultuous time for the industry, Go aims to be a steady hand on the tiller. Our goal is to keep Go grounded in its foundational principles of simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and an unwavering commitment to compatibility, while adapting to modern hardware, production workloads, and developer workflows. Increasingly, our investments serve a dual purpose: what helps human engineers write, understand, and maintain reliable Go code at scale also provides the guardrails and authoritative context that AI coding assistants and agents need to be effective. Core language and library improvements In the language itself, Go 1.26 and 1.27 addressed several long-standing restrictions in generics and everyday Go syntax, guided by years of real-world experience. entries.summary: Go 1.27 introduces new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages.
entries.text: The Go Blog A new Go API for JSON Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil 4 November 2026 Introduction JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago! Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes. After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with encoding/json and introducing the new packages. Problems with encoding/json Overall, encoding/json has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings. entries.summary: How the Go team responded to the eMudhra certificate compromise with our first-ever URGENT track security release.
entries.text: The Go Blog Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident Roland Shoemaker, on behalf of the Go Security team 26 October 2026 On October 19, the Go team initiated an expedited security release to protect Go users and their applications from a critical public key infrastructure (PKI) compromise involving certificates issued by eMudhra. Within approximately seven and a half hours of being notified, we shipped a targeted patch, which was included in our first-ever URGENT track security release. Here is the context behind the incident, why Go stepped in at the runtime level to protect our users and how our incident response unfolded. eMudhra Incident On October 17, Mozilla added eight intermediate certificates (six used for TLS, and two used for code signing) issued by a root certificate controlled by eMudhra to OneCRL, effectively blocking their usage in Firefox. Soon after, a number of security researchers noticed this and began investigating what might’ve caused this. On October 19, the Go Security team was made aware of these investigations and their conclusions, which showed that the keys associated with these intermediates were trivially weak, allowing recovery of the private keys in microseconds. Due to the fact that the eMudhra root certificate was present in most trusted root programs, recovering the private keys would allow any attacker to sign arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain name, without the usual requirement to show proof of control of said domain nam

entries.summary: Share your experience with Go in the 2026 Go Developer Survey, open through November 3.
entries.text: The Go Blog Help set Go's priorities for next year Cameron Balahan, on behalf of the Go team 21 October 2026 Hi Gophers! The 2026 Go Developer Survey is now open. We run this survey every year to understand how you use Go and the challenges you face. Your answers directly shape how we plan and prioritize our work. Last year, 5,379 of you responded, and your top frustration was making sure your code follows best practices and Go idioms (33% of respondents). Since then, we shipped a rewritten go fix in Go 1.26 that automatically modernizes your code, and added more modernizers in Go 1.27. You can read everything we learned in the 2025 results. Take the survey here. It’s open through November 3, takes about 10–20 minutes, and every question is optional. We’ll share the results on this blog in early 2027. Please share the survey with your colleagues, friends, and online communities—the more Go developers we hear from, the better we understand what you need. Thank you for helping shape the future of Go! Next article: Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident Previous article: Interactive refactoring in gopls Blog Index

entries.summary: Introducing interactive refactoring in gopls and the LSP: a new capability that brings dynamic, multi-step refactorings into your favorite editor.
entries.text: The Go Blog Interactive refactoring in gopls Hongxiang Jiang 16 October 2026 When editing code in a modern IDE or editor, developers rely on its refactoring features to automate common transformations. Today, we are excited to introduce interactive refactoring in gopls, powered by a new capability we are proposing for the Language Server Protocol (LSP) that brings dynamic, multi-step dialogs directly into your favorite editor. Crucially, we designed this capability (in collaboration with the Dart team) not just for Go, but as an open standard for all programming languages and editor ecosystems. Working support is already available in gopls v0.24.0 and the official Go extension for VS Code v0.56.0. What is the Language Server Protocol (LSP)? The LSP is an open standard that decouples language-specific features from specific text editors. As you navigate and edit code, your editor (such as VS Code, Neovim, or Emacs) and a language server (like gopls) engage in a continuous JSON-RPC exchange to provide features like autocomplete, hover documentation, diagnostics, and code actions. Multi-step code transformation Today, almost every code transformation in the LSP is like a function of no parameters: you trigger the operation, and the server immediately computes the edits. (Renaming a symbol is the sole exception: because it is a function of one parameter, the desired new name, it required its own dedicated PrepareRename RPC in the protocol.) entries.summary: Go 1.27 includes a change to the HTTP client that can make programs sending many sequential HTTP/1 requests significantly faster.
entries.text: The Go Blog Better HTTP/1 connection reuse Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil 14 October 2026 Take a look at the following function: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code. Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds. That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible? The cost of establishing HTTP connections To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request. Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this: TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK, establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT). TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT. entries.summary: Go 1.27 introduces experimental arch-specific SIMD vector APIs
entries.text: The Go Blog Arch-specific SIMD in Go Junyang Shao and David Chase 2 October 2026 Since Go 1.26, we have supported an experimental amd64 SIMD API. Now in Go 1.27, we support two more architectures: arm64 and wasm. The new APIs can be accessed by setting GOEXPERIMENT=simd when building a program. They are defined in the simd/archsimd package. archsimd is the lower-level infrastructure that simd builds on, essentially the intrinsics layer in other languages. For exotic operations that only exist on a specific architecture, users can access them by transitioning from simd to archsimd (via ToArch and <Types>FromArch). For details, please refer to the simd blog post. For readers with prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics in other languages, you might find that our archsimd API does not directly mirror the underlying hardware instructions: We give our APIs sensible names: e.g., instead of _mm512_slli_epi64, we just call it ShiftAllLeft. We leave some architecture details to compiler optimizations rather than exposing them in the API: e.g., instead of _mm512_maskz_add_ps(m, x, y), we optimize x.Add(y).Masked(m) into the same instruction. These design decisions make our APIs smaller and more accessible, and they also happily make the simd implementation much easier. For readers without prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics, we hope our low-level API is a natural and pleasant journey for you. Please share your feedback and comments. Anything about usability, performance, etc., is appreciated
entries.title: Arch-specific SIMD in Go

entries.summary: Go 1.27 adds an experimental platform-agnostic SIMD API
entries.text: The Go Blog Platform-independent SIMD in Go David Chase and Junyang Shao 24 September 2026 Go 1.26 and 1.27 include experimental APIs for Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) operations. SIMD is a native feature of many modern CPUs that allows software to perform uniform operations across vectors of data very quickly, such as adding 8 pairs of float64 values in a single instruction. It can significantly speed up many computationally-intensive tasks, ranging from cryptography to data processing to AI. In fact, Go’s Green Tea garbage collector even makes use of SIMD to accelerate scanning memory for live objects. Prior to these new experimental APIs, the only way to access this functionality from Go was by writing Go assembly. This was only worth it for truly performance-critical compute kernels, which meant plenty of software that could benefit from SIMD simply left a lot of the CPU unused. Go 1.26 introduced a SIMD API for amd64, and Go 1.27 added APIs for arm64 (specifically NEON) and wasm. However, a basic challenge for a SIMD API is the enormous variation between platforms, not simply in what operations they support, but even in how vectors are represented. Some platforms provide fixed-size vectors, typically between 128 bits and 512 bits, while on others the vector size isn’t known at build time and must be queried when the program starts. To provide full access to the breadth of these platforms, these APIs live in an architecture-dependent archsimd package. But Go 1.2

entries.summary: Go 1.27 improves performance of small allocations using size-specialized allocation functions.
entries.text: The Go Blog Size-Specialized Memory Allocation Michael Matloob 16 September 2026 Go 1.27 includes faster memory allocation for allocations of 80 bytes or fewer. Allocations can be up to 20-30% faster, making allocation-heavy programs up to 1% faster. The Go runtime improves the performance of those allocations by adding specialized functions that are used to allocate certain sizes. These specialized functions can then make certain assumptions that make them faster and easier to optimize. This blog post will explain how this works and how it makes your programs faster. Heap allocations are created by the runtime’s mallocgc function, which requires the size of the allocation and whether it contains pointers. When the compiler determines that an object escapes to the heap or otherwise needs to be dynamically allocated, it inserts a call to newobject, which is a simple wrapper function that extracts the size of the object and whether it contains pointers and passes those to mallocgc. These two pieces of information determine most of the work that the allocator needs to do. The size is important because the allocator defines ranges of sizes called “size classes”. For most allocations that are not too large and not too small, it will return a block of memory from a list of free objects that are all sized to the maximum size of the size class. entries.summary: Go 1.27 includes new goroutine leak profiles.
entries.text: The Go Blog Goroutine Leak Profiles Vlad Saioc 2 September 2026 Go’s concurrency features are powerful and easy to use, but that same ease can sometimes lead even seasoned developers to make mistakes. Fortunately, the Go ecosystem comes equipped with useful tools for debugging, e.g., the race detector, but even existing tools may miss some concurrency bugs, such as the topic of this article, the goroutine leak. Goroutines synchronize or exchange information via shared concurrency primitives, e.g., channels, locks, and wait groups. While communicating, goroutines often block on these primitives, as in, wait until some condition is met; ubiquitous examples include waiting to acquire a held mutex, or receive a message over a channel. Goroutines can also block on operating system operations, like reading from a network socket or a file. We may consider a goroutine leaked if it is blocked, but the conditions needed to unblock it can never be met. Over time, an accumulation of leaked goroutines degrades performance through excessive memory usage (by the leaked goroutines themselves or the memory they reference), as well as CPU usage from the garbage collector, especially if GOMEMLIMIT is in use. Goroutine leaks can be notoriously difficult to detect. In unit testing, the most significant breakthroughs include the open-source library goleak, which can instrument individual tests to signal any un-terminated goroutines after the test wraps up as suspicious.
